tagline: A striped illumination pattern mixes sample frequencies that the objective cannot pass down into its passband (moiré), and computation moves them back, giving about twice the widefield resolution in x, y and z.
principle: A widefield fluorescence microscope is a low-pass filter: its optical transfer function (OTF) is zero beyond the cut-off spatial frequency k0 = 2NA/λ, so any detail finer than about λ/(2NA) is simply not transmitted. The image is the product of the dye distribution and the illumination, and in Fourier space a product becomes a convolution. If the illumination is a sinusoid of spatial frequency p, its spectrum is three delta peaks (at 0 and ±p), so the recorded image contains three copies of the sample spectrum, shifted by 0, +p and -p, each filtered by the same OTF. Sample information originally at k ± p now sits at k, inside the passband. In real space this is the moiré effect: two fine patterns beat to give a coarse one.

To use this, the three overlapping copies must be separated. Shifting the stripe phase (three phases for 2D SIM, five for 3D SIM) gives a set of linear equations that can be solved for each component. The pattern is then rotated (usually three orientations, 60° apart) so that the extended region covers all directions. Each component is shifted back to its true position in frequency space, the pieces are weighted and combined with a generalised Wiener filter, apodised and inverse-transformed.

Because the stripe pattern is itself made by the objective, its frequency cannot exceed about 2NA/λ_exc. The largest recoverable frequency is therefore roughly k0 + p ≈ 2k0, which is why linear SIM is limited to about a twofold gain (around 100-120 nm laterally for green emission at NA 1.4). In 3D SIM three beams (orders 0 and ±1) interfere, giving a pattern that is also modulated along z. This fills the 'missing cone' of the widefield OTF and doubles axial resolution as well, at the cost of 15 raw images per plane (5 phases x 3 angles).

Going beyond twofold requires a nonlinear response so that the effective pattern contains higher harmonics: saturated excitation (SSIM) or reversibly photoswitchable proteins (patterned activation NL-SIM) in principle give unlimited resolution and have reached about 50-60 nm. TIRF-SIM and grazing-incidence SIM use high-angle beams to push the illumination frequency to its maximum for fast imaging near the coverslip.

Reconstruction needs accurate values of the pattern frequency, angle, phase and modulation depth, which are estimated from the raw data themselves. When these estimates, the OTF, or the sample (motion, bleaching, out-of-focus haze, refractive-index mismatch) deviate from the model, the algorithm produces structured artefacts rather than just noise. SIM works with ordinary dyes and fluorescent proteins and at relatively low light dose, which is why it is a mainstay of live-cell super-resolution.
light_path: A laser (often several lines combined) is delivered by fibre, sometimes through a speckle reducer.
The beam hits a pattern generator: a phase grating, a spatial light modulator (SLM) or a digital micromirror device (DMD), which produces diffraction orders.
A mask in a Fourier plane passes only the 0 and ±1 orders (3D SIM) or only ±1 (2D/TIRF-SIM).
A polarisation rotator (or liquid crystal) keeps the light s-polarised (perpendicular to the plane of the beams) for each pattern angle, which maximises stripe contrast at high NA.
The orders are focused to points near the edge of the objective back focal plane, emerge as plane waves at steep angles and interfere in the sample to form the stripe pattern.
Fluorescence is collected by the same objective, separated by a dichroic and emission filter, and imaged on an sCMOS or EMCCD camera.
The pattern is stepped through 3 or 5 phases and 3 angles, giving 9 or 15 raw frames per plane (per z-step in 3D).
Software estimates the pattern parameters, separates and shifts the frequency components, combines them with a Wiener filter and outputs the reconstruction.

resolution.xy: ~100-120 nm linear SIM; ~50-60 nm nonlinear SIM
resolution.why: The illumination stripes are themselves diffraction-limited, so at most one extra passband's worth of frequencies (about 2NA/λ) can be shifted in, giving a maximum of ~2x; going further needs a nonlinear sample response.

strengths: Works with ordinary dyes and fluorescent proteins; multicolour is straightforward.
Modest light dose and fast acquisition compared with STED or SMLM, so suitable for live cells.
Doubles axial as well as lateral resolution (3D SIM), with optical sectioning.
Widefield camera detection gives large fields of view.
limitations: Resolution gain is capped at ~2x for linear SIM.
Reconstruction is model-based and produces characteristic artefacts if raw data are imperfect.
Sensitive to spherical aberration, refractive-index mismatch and thick, hazy samples.
Moving samples blur between phase steps; intensity quantitation after reconstruction is not straightforward.
best_for: Organelle morphology and contacts (mitochondrial cristae, ER, Golgi) in live cells.
Cytoskeletal networks, synaptic and centrosome architecture in fixed cells.
Nuclear organisation (chromatin, nuclear pores, lamina) with 3D SIM.
Fast dynamics near the membrane with TIRF-SIM.
sample_prep: Use #1.5H coverslips, thoroughly cleaned to remove fluorescent debris. Label densely and brightly with photostable dyes or bright fluorescent proteins; high signal and low background are essential because modulation contrast drives reconstruction quality. Mount fixed samples in a medium whose refractive index matches the immersion oil (e.g. hardening glycerol-based mountants or ProLong Glass-type media), and keep the sample thin and close to the coverslip. For live cells use phenol-red-free medium, a stage-top incubator and, ideally, a silicone or water objective for deeper planes.
tips: Tune spherical aberration first: choose immersion oil of the right refractive index (oils are sold in steps, e.g. 1.512-1.518) by imaging sub-diffraction beads and checking that the axial PSF is symmetric.

Run SIMcheck (Fiji) on raw data before trusting any reconstruction: it reports bleaching and intensity fluctuations between angles, motion, modulation contrast-to-noise ratio (MCNR) per pixel, and in the reconstruction shows Fourier-space coverage, negative-value histograms and spherical-aberration mismatch.
Aim for MCNR well above ~8 in structures of interest; low MCNR means the reconstruction there is mostly noise amplification.
Measure the OTF with a bead on the same system and settings (and channel) rather than using a theoretical one.
Do not set the Wiener parameter too low to make images look sharper; it inflates noise into false fine structure.
Register channels using multicolour beads imaged in SIM mode; chromatic offsets of tens of nm matter at this resolution.
Keep total bleaching across the acquisition low (SIMcheck shows it), and acquire with fewer z-planes if needed.
pitfalls: Honeycomb or hexagonal patterns in the background: often from out-of-focus light, low modulation or a too-low Wiener parameter. They are periodic at the pattern frequency, which SIMcheck's Fourier views reveal.
Hammer-finish or stripy texture and ghost repeats of structures: wrong estimates of pattern phase or angle, or pattern drift between frames.
Ghost images above and below bright objects in z: spherical aberration from mismatched oil or mounting medium.
Sharp-looking but fake fine filaments in noisy regions: noise amplification by the reconstruction.
Blurring or doubled edges in live cells: sample motion during the 9-15 raw frames.
Reduced quality deep in tissue: aberrations and haze lower modulation contrast.

quiz.q: Explain in Fourier terms why SIM doubles resolution and why it cannot do better without nonlinearity.
quiz.a: Multiplying the sample by a sinusoid convolves its spectrum with peaks at ±p, shifting high frequencies into the OTF support. Since the pattern is made through the same optics, p cannot exceed ~2NA/λ, so the extended support reaches at most about twice the cut-off. A nonlinear response adds harmonics at 2p, 3p and so on, which extends support further.

quiz.q: A user brings you a SIM image with a honeycomb pattern. How do you troubleshoot?
quiz.a: Look at the raw data with SIMcheck: check modulation contrast (MCNR), bleaching and angle intensity balance; look at the reconstructed Fourier transform for spots at the pattern frequency. Typical causes are out-of-focus haze or thick samples, a mismatched OTF, wrong parameter estimates or too low a Wiener constant. Fixes: thinner sample or better mounting, correct immersion oil, measured OTF, higher Wiener parameter, more signal.

quiz.q: Why do 3D SIM systems use 5 phases and 2D systems 3?
quiz.a: In 3D SIM the 0 and ±1 orders interfere, giving five frequency components (0, ±p/2 axially modulated, and ±p), so five independent phase steps are needed to separate them; 2D SIM has only three components.

quiz.q: When would you recommend SIM over STED or SMLM?
quiz.a: For live or multicolour imaging where ~2x resolution suffices and speed, low light dose and standard labels matter, e.g. organelle dynamics or 3D nuclear structure. Choose STED or SMLM when you need sub-60 nm resolution or molecular counting.

tagline: A doughnut-shaped depletion beam forces excited molecules back to the ground state everywhere except at its central zero, shrinking the effective focal spot to tens of nanometres.
principle: STED (stimulated emission depletion) is a point-scanning method. A diffraction-limited excitation spot is overlaid with a red-shifted depletion beam shaped like a doughnut, with an intensity zero at its centre. In the doughnut, the depletion beam drives excited molecules down to a high vibrational level of the ground state by stimulated emission, at the wavelength of the depletion light, which is filtered out. Only molecules at the zero remain able to fluoresce spontaneously.

The fraction of molecules that survive depletion falls roughly exponentially with depletion intensity, η ≈ exp(−I/Is), where the saturation intensity Is is the intensity at which stimulated emission competes equally with spontaneous decay (Is ≈ 1/(σ_STED τ) in photon flux units). Because the doughnut intensity grows away from the zero, any intensity well above Is confines fluorescence to a region whose width shrinks as 1/√(I/Is). Resolution is therefore not limited by diffraction in principle; it is limited by how much light the sample and dye can tolerate and by how perfect the zero is.

The lateral doughnut is made with a helical (vortex) 0-2π phase plate on a circularly polarised beam; a phase plate with a central π ring creates a 'bottle' beam that confines the spot along z. Combining both gives 3D STED. Pulsed depletion (sub-ns pulses timed just after excitation) is most efficient; continuous-wave STED works but benefits from time-gated detection (gated STED), which discards the photons emitted in the first ns before depletion has acted.

The same principle, called RESOLFT, applies to any reversible saturable transition. With reversibly switchable fluorescent proteins the switching intensities are orders of magnitude lower than for stimulated emission, which is gentler on live cells but slower. STED is also combined with FCS (STED-FCS) to measure diffusion at sub-diffraction scales.

The resolution gain comes at a cost: very high local intensities (typically MW to GW per cm² peak), photobleaching through excited-state absorption from the depletion beam, and the need for dyes with good stimulated-emission cross-sections at available depletion lines (592, 660 and especially 775 nm).
light_path: A pulsed excitation laser (e.g. 640 nm) and a red-shifted depletion laser (e.g. 775 nm, sub-ns pulses) are combined; their pulses are synchronised so depletion arrives just after excitation.
The depletion beam passes through a vortex phase plate (or SLM) and quarter-wave plate to form a circularly polarised doughnut; a π-ring plate adds z-confinement.
Both beams are co-aligned through a scan head (galvanometers, sometimes with a resonant mirror) and focused by a high-NA oil or silicone objective.
Fluorescence returns through the objective, is descanned, separated from both lasers by dichroics and notch filters, passes a confocal pinhole and is detected by an APD or hybrid detector.
Time-gated detection rejects early photons; the image is built pixel by pixel, often with line accumulation.

resolution.xy: ~30-80 nm routinely in cells; <20 nm under ideal conditions
resolution.z: ~100-150 nm with 3D (z-donut) STED; confocal-like (~500-600 nm) with xy STED only
resolution.why: Set by the achievable I/Is, which is limited by photobleaching and phototoxicity, and by the depth of the doughnut zero, which aberrations degrade.

strengths: Resolution is achieved optically, without reconstruction or post-processing.
Works with standard immunostaining and commercial dyes; fast for small fields.
Optical sectioning from the confocal pinhole; can image several microns deep with adaptive optics.
Resolution tunable on the fly by depletion power.
limitations: High light doses cause bleaching and phototoxicity, limiting live and 3D imaging.
Point scanning is slow for large fields, especially at the small pixel sizes required.
Dye choice constrained by depletion wavelengths; multicolour typically limited to 2-3 colours.
Sensitive to aberrations, which fill the doughnut zero and destroy resolution with depth.
best_for: Synaptic protein nanoclusters and vesicle pools.
Cytoskeletal periodicities, e.g. the ~190 nm actin-spectrin rings in axons.
Nanoscale organisation of mitochondrial and nuclear pore proteins.
Lipid and protein nanodomain diffusion with STED-FCS.
sample_prep: Use bright, photostable dyes with efficient depletion at the instrument's STED line (e.g. organic dyes on secondary antibodies or nanobodies; SiR or JF dyes with SNAP/Halo tags for live cells). Mount in a medium with refractive index matched to the objective (e.g. TDE- or glycerol-based mountants for oil) to keep the doughnut zero clean, and use #1.5H coverslips. Avoid DAPI or other blue-absorbing stains that absorb the depletion light, and avoid mounting media with antifade components that quench the chosen dye.
tips: Check doughnut quality and co-alignment with gold beads imaged in reflection or with fluorescent beads; a filled zero shows as a halo and loss of resolution.
Increase STED power stepwise and watch bleaching; often 50-70% of maximum gives the best signal-to-resolution compromise.
Use time gating and line accumulation instead of long pixel dwells; adaptive schemes (RESCue, DyMIN) switch off the depletion beam where no signal is present and reduce bleaching substantially.
Pick pixel sizes at Nyquist for the expected resolution (≈ resolution/2.3) but no smaller, since every pixel costs dose.
For multicolour, acquire the redder channel first and use dyes depleted by the same STED line; check chromatic registration with multicolour beads.
Deconvolution with a measured STED PSF often gives a further, honest improvement in contrast.
pitfalls: Rapid photobleaching, especially in z-stacks and 3D STED; later frames look dimmer and coarser.
Re-excitation background: the depletion beam can directly excite the dye (anti-Stokes excitation), producing a blurry background that time gating or background subtraction must remove.
Resolution varies across the image and with depth because of aberrations; quote resolution from isolated features or FRC, not from the best spot.
Apparent clusters that are labelling or antibody artefacts, which STED reveals more clearly than confocal.
Sample heating and drift during long scans.

quiz.q: Write down the STED resolution formula and explain each term.
quiz.a: d ≈ λ/(2NA√(1+I/Is)). λ/(2NA) is the diffraction limit; I is the peak depletion intensity at the doughnut crest and Is the dye's saturation intensity. Higher I/Is confines fluorescence to a smaller region around the zero.

quiz.q: Why is 775 nm so popular as a depletion wavelength?
quiz.a: It sits on the red tail of the emission of red dyes such as STAR RED or ATTO 647N, giving efficient stimulated emission with little direct excitation, it is available as high-power pulsed fibre lasers, and it is gentler on cells than shorter wavelengths. It also allows two colours depleted by one beam.

quiz.q: A user says resolution looks no better than confocal deep in their tissue. Why?
quiz.a: Refractive-index mismatch and tissue aberrations fill the doughnut zero, so depletion also suppresses the centre. Remedies are a matched immersion objective (silicone or glycerol), correction collar adjustment, adaptive optics and imaging closer to the coverslip.

quiz.q: How do STED and RESOLFT differ?
quiz.a: Both use a saturable transition and a pattern with a zero. STED uses stimulated emission, which needs very high intensity because it competes with ns fluorescence; RESOLFT uses long-lived switchable states, so far lower intensities work, but switching takes longer and imaging is slower.

tagline: If only a sparse random subset of fluorophores emits at any moment, each can be localized far more precisely than the PSF width, and accumulating many thousands of frames builds a nanometre-scale image.
principle: The image of a single emitter is the PSF, about 250 nm wide, but its centre can be estimated to a precision that improves with the number of photons collected. In the simplest limit the precision is σ ≈ s/√N, where s is the PSF standard deviation (~100-130 nm) and N the detected photons, so 1000 photons give ~4 nm in the absence of background. Pixelation, background and camera noise worsen this; Thompson and later Mortensen derived the full expressions, and maximum-likelihood fitting approaches the Cramér-Rao lower bound.

Localization only works when PSFs do not overlap, so the vast majority of labels must be dark in any frame. PALM uses photoactivatable or photoconvertible fluorescent proteins (PA-GFP, mEos, Dendra2) switched on stochastically by low-level 405 nm light. STORM originally used Cy3-Cy5 activator-reporter pairs; dSTORM and GSDIM drive conventional dyes such as Alexa Fluor 647 into long-lived dark states (radical anions or triplet) with intense red light in a thiol-containing reducing buffer, from which they return stochastically. The localizations from 10^4-10^5 frames are rendered as a point cloud or histogram.

Resolution in the final image depends on more than precision: label density must satisfy a Nyquist-type criterion (mean label spacing at most half the resolution sought), and linkage error from primary-secondary antibodies (~10-20 nm) or fluorescent protein fusions adds to the uncertainty. Fourier ring correlation (FRC) gives a data-driven resolution estimate.

3D is achieved by encoding z in the PSF shape: a cylindrical lens introduces astigmatism so the spot becomes elliptical above or below focus (~50-60 nm z precision over ~800 nm), or biplane, double-helix and tetrapod PSFs are used. Interferometric 4Pi approaches (iPALM, 4Pi-SMS) reach ~10-20 nm axially.

SMLM data are lists of molecules with coordinates and photon counts, which enables cluster analysis (DBSCAN, Ripley's K, pair-correlation) and counting. But because each fluorophore can blink several times, the number of localizations is not the number of molecules; this is the central quantitative difficulty.
light_path: High-power lasers (e.g. 640-647 nm at 1-10 kW/cm² for dSTORM) and a weak 405 nm activation laser are combined, expanded and focused to the back focal plane of a high-NA (1.4-1.5) TIRF objective.
Illumination is set to TIRF, HILO or epi depending on depth; flat-top beam shaping improves uniformity.
A focus-lock system (IR beam reflected from the coverslip) holds focus over long acquisitions.
Emission passes a multiband dichroic and emission filter; for 3D a weak cylindrical lens is placed before the camera.
An EMCCD or sCMOS camera records 10,000-100,000 frames at 10-50 ms exposure with ~100-160 nm projected pixels.
Software detects candidate spots, fits each (Gaussian MLE), filters by photons and width, corrects drift and renders the image.

strengths: Highest routine resolution among fluorescence methods available in standard labs (~20 nm).
Simple widefield/TIRF hardware.
Produces coordinate lists suitable for cluster analysis, counting and colocalization statistics.
Single-molecule information (photons, blinking) aids quantitation and live sptPALM.
limitations: Slow: minutes per image, so mostly fixed samples.
Requires harsh buffers and high laser power for dye blinking.
Multicolour is harder because the best dye (Alexa 647) is far-red; other dyes blink less well.
Quantitation complicated by blinking, incomplete labelling and photoconversion efficiency.

Nuclear pore and centriole architecture, often used as resolution standards.

sample_prep: Fix with PFA (adding 0.1-0.2% glutaraldehyde preserves fine structure, quench with NaBH4), permeabilize and block thoroughly. Use high-density, specific labelling: directly labelled primaries, nanobodies or SNAP/Halo tags reduce linkage error. For dSTORM use Alexa 647 or CF647 (Cy3B or CF568 as second colour) and image in fresh oxygen-scavenging, thiol buffer in a sealed chamber; the buffer acidifies and loses performance after about 1-2 hours. For PALM use mEos3.2 or PA-mCherry fusions expressed at near-endogenous levels. Add fiducial markers (gold nanoparticles or multicolour beads) for drift correction.
tips: Correct drift with fiducials fixed to the coverslip or with redundant cross-correlation on the localizations; check residual drift on fiducials is below a few nm.
Keep the active emitter density low enough that PSFs rarely overlap (roughly < 1 per µm² per frame for single-emitter fitting); raise 405 nm power gradually as molecules are used up.
Use maximum-likelihood fitting with a camera noise model; for sCMOS, calibrate per-pixel offset, variance and gain.
Merge localizations that reappear at the same position within a short dark-time tolerance to reduce repeated counting, and report how this was done.
Estimate resolution with FRC and show widefield images alongside to confirm structures are real.
Test the buffer on a reference sample (microtubules) before precious samples.
pitfalls: Overcounting: one fluorophore blinking many times produces a cluster of localizations that looks like a nanocluster of molecules. Recognise it with pair-correlation analysis, blinking statistics and controls with monomeric reference proteins.
Overlapping emitters at high density give false localizations between real molecules, merging or bridging structures; use multi-emitter fitting or lower density.
Incomplete labelling or FP maturation leads to undercounting and patchy structures mistaken for clusters.
Uncorrected drift smears structures; chromatic shifts misregister colours.
Fixed dipoles (e.g. rigidly bound dyes) give biased localizations of tens of nm, especially out of focus.
Cluster analyses depend strongly on parameters; random-distribution simulations at the same density are an essential control.

quiz.q: How do you estimate localization precision and how does it differ from resolution?
quiz.a: Precision is the standard deviation of repeated localizations of one molecule, estimated from the Thompson/Mortensen formula, the Cramér-Rao bound, or experimentally from repeated localizations of the same molecule (nearest-neighbour analysis in consecutive frames). Resolution additionally depends on label density, linkage error and drift; FRC is one measure.

quiz.q: What goes into a dSTORM buffer and why?
quiz.a: An oxygen scavenger (glucose oxidase and catalase with glucose, or PCA/PCD) removes oxygen that would quench the dark state and bleach the dye; a primary thiol such as MEA or βME reduces the excited dye to a long-lived dark radical state; pH ~8 helps. 405 nm light accelerates return to the on state.

quiz.q: Your SMLM data show protein nanoclusters. How do you convince yourself they are real?
quiz.a: Check blinking-induced overcounting with pair-correlation and with monomeric controls labelled the same way; compare to simulations of random distributions at matched density and blinking statistics; check fiducial drift; use alternative labels; confirm cluster sizes are larger than the precision and repeatable.

quiz.q: EMCCD or sCMOS for SMLM?
quiz.a: EMCCD has near-zero read noise but an excess noise factor of √2 that effectively halves the photons; sCMOS has low read noise (~1-2 e⁻), larger fields and faster frame rates, but pixel-dependent noise that must be calibrated. For bright dyes sCMOS is now usually preferred.

tagline: Short dye-labelled DNA strands bind transiently to complementary docking strands on the target, so the blinking needed for localization comes from hybridization kinetics rather than dye photophysics.
principle: In PAINT (points accumulation for imaging in nanoscale topography), labelled probes diffusing in solution bind briefly to the target and are imaged as fixed spots, while the freely diffusing probes are too fast to form a spot and contribute only a diffuse background. DNA-PAINT implements this with a short single-stranded 'docking' oligo (typically 8-10 nt) attached to the target via an antibody, nanobody or tag, and a complementary dye-labelled 'imager' strand in the buffer.

Binding is a reversible bimolecular reaction. The mean bright time is τ_b = 1/k_off, set by the duplex length and salt (about 0.3-1 s for 9 bp), and the mean dark time is τ_d = 1/(k_on·c), set by imager concentration c and association rate k_on (~10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹ for classic sequences, ~10⁷ for optimized repetitive sequences). Because blinking is programmed, it can be tuned independently of the dye, and because the imager pool is constantly replenished, the target is effectively immune to photobleaching.

Each binding event collects many photons (long exposures of 100-300 ms with bright dyes like Cy3B or ATTO 655), so localization precision can reach ~1-5 nm. Sequence orthogonality allows multiplexing: in Exchange-PAINT the imager is washed out and replaced with another sequence, so one dye and one channel can image many targets without chromatic aberration.

The predictable kinetics also allow counting. In qPAINT the mean dark time at a site is inversely proportional to the number of docking strands there, n = 1/(k_on · c · τ_d), calibrated on single docking sites. RESI (resolution enhancement by sequential imaging) images neighbouring targets with different sequences in separate rounds, so each target's many localizations can be averaged to Ångström precision.

The main costs are speed and background. Free imagers fluoresce, so imaging needs TIRF or HILO and a low imager concentration, and that low concentration makes binding sparse and acquisitions long (tens of minutes to hours). Optimized repetitive docking sequences and higher salt speed this up 10-100 fold.

quiz.q: How do imager concentration and k_on determine your acquisition?
quiz.a: The dark time per site is 1/(k_on·c). At k_on = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹ and c = 1 nM, each site binds roughly every 1000 s, so with many sites per diffraction area you get sparse blinking but need long acquisitions to sample each site several times. Raising c speeds it up but increases background and overlap.

quiz.q: Why is DNA-PAINT resistant to photobleaching?
quiz.a: The dye is on the imager, not the target; a bleached imager simply unbinds and is replaced from a large pool in solution, so the docking site keeps producing events.

quiz.q: How would you distinguish specific from nonspecific localizations?
quiz.a: Specific sites show repeated binding with bright times matching the expected duplex lifetime and dark times following the expected distribution; nonspecific sticking shows single or anomalously long events. Kinetic filtering and no-docking-strand controls separate them.

quiz.q: Compare DNA-PAINT with dSTORM.

tagline: Instead of fitting a camera image, MINFLUX localizes a single emitter by probing it with an excitation pattern that has an intensity zero, so few photons give nanometre precision.
principle: In camera-based localization the information comes from the shape of the PSF, whose width s (~100 nm) sets precision σ ≈ s/√N. MINFLUX reverses the roles: a doughnut-shaped excitation beam with a central zero is placed at a few known positions around the expected molecule location (for example three on a circle of diameter L plus one at the centre), and the photon counts at each position are recorded. Near the zero the excitation intensity rises quadratically with distance, so the ratios of counts encode the molecule's position very sensitively.

The Cramér-Rao bound for this estimate scales with L instead of s: precision improves as L/√N, so shrinking the probing pattern makes each photon more informative. Measurements are done iteratively: a coarse localization defines a new centre, L is reduced, and the process repeats, zooming in until L is a few tens of nm. In this regime 1-3 nm precision is obtained with a few hundred to a thousand photons.

Because the zero of the beam keeps the emitter in low light, MINFLUX is photon efficient, which also makes it attractive for tracking: a molecule can be followed with nm precision at sub-millisecond time resolution, as done for kinesin stepping in vitro and in cells.

Like SMLM it still needs only one emitter active within the probed region, so it relies on photoswitchable or photoactivatable dyes and proteins, or on DNA-PAINT binding. Acquisitions are slow (tens of minutes to hours for small fields), and the instrument must be stabilised to sub-nm with active feedback from reflected fiducials.

MINSTED is a related approach: it scans a STED-sharpened excitation spot in a circle around the molecule, recentres on it and progressively increases STED power to shrink the spot, reaching similar 1-3 nm precision with a different trade-off between photon count and background.
light_path: Excitation laser (e.g. 560 or 640 nm) passes electro-optic deflectors that position the beam within the focal region at µs speed, and a phase mask or SLM that shapes the 2D doughnut or 3D bottle beam.
A separate 405 nm activation beam switches on single molecules; galvanometer scanners position the region of interest.
The objective focuses the pattern; an IR beam reflected from gold nanoparticle fiducials feeds an active stabilisation loop to correct drift in three axes at sub-nm level.
Fluorescence is descanned through a confocal pinhole and counted on APDs for each beam position.
A real-time controller estimates the position after each iteration, recentres the pattern and shrinks L until the final iteration.

tagline: Analysing the statistics or radial symmetry of intensity fluctuations in a stack of ordinary images gives sharper images from blinking emitters, without the need to isolate single molecules.
principle: When emitters blink independently, the fluctuations of different molecules are uncorrelated, while the fluctuations at neighbouring pixels caused by the same molecule are correlated. SOFI (super-resolution optical fluctuation imaging) exploits this by computing temporal cumulants of each pixel's intensity trace. The n-th order cumulant is a sum over emitters of the PSF raised to the n-th power, weighted by brightness to the n-th power and a blinking term. Raising a Gaussian PSF to the n-th power narrows it by √n, and with Fourier reweighting the gain can approach n.

Cross-cumulants between neighbouring pixels create 'virtual pixels' between the real ones, and using a time lag τ > 0 removes uncorrelated noise such as shot noise and camera read noise, which only correlate at zero lag. SOFI also suppresses static background and out-of-focus light that does not fluctuate.

SRRF (super-resolution radial fluctuations) takes a different route: in each frame it computes on a finer grid how strongly local intensity gradients converge on a point (radiality), which peaks at the centres of emitters; temporal analysis of the radiality stack (mean or autocorrelation) then gives the final image. eSRRF added data-driven optimization of parameters and 3D extension.

Fluctuation methods tolerate high emitter densities and can work with standard fluorescent proteins and dyes at low illumination, giving live-cell compatible images from a few hundred frames. The price is that the outputs are nonlinear in brightness (an n-th order cumulant scales with brightness^n), so dim structures next to bright ones can vanish, and the resolution gain is moderate and depends on blinking statistics.

Because the algorithms can create sharp-looking structures that are not there, quality control is essential. SQUIRREL compares the super-resolved image, convolved back to diffraction-limited resolution, against the widefield reference to produce an error map and global metrics (resolution-scaled error and Pearson correlation).

tagline: Anchoring biomolecules into a swellable hydrogel and then expanding it physically separates structures, so a conventional microscope resolves features about 4-20 times smaller.
principle: Expansion microscopy (ExM) improves resolution by making the sample bigger rather than the optics better. Biomolecules or labels are chemically linked to a polyelectrolyte gel (sodium acrylate co-polymerised with acrylamide and crosslinked by bis-acrylamide) that is formed throughout the fixed specimen. The sample's mechanical integrity is then disrupted by protease digestion (proteinase K) or by heat and detergent denaturation, and the gel is placed in water. Electrostatic repulsion of the charged polymer and osmotic swelling expand it isotropically about 4-4.5 fold in each dimension (~70-90 fold in volume).

The effective resolution is the microscope resolution divided by the expansion factor: a 250 nm confocal becomes ~60 nm, and combined with SIM, STED or SMLM can approach 10-20 nm or better. Iterative ExM (re-embedding and expanding again) and gel recipes giving ~10 fold expansion in one step push the factor to ~10-20.

The method's accuracy depends on isotropy. Distortion is measured by imaging the same cell before and after expansion and comparing with non-rigid registration; good protocols give root-mean-square errors of a few percent over length scales of microns. Tissues with tough extracellular matrix or cell walls need harsher or longer digestion.

Labels can be applied before gelation (antibodies with anchoring via AcX, as in proExM) or after expansion (U-ExM, magnified analysis of the proteome, MAP-like protocols), where epitopes are preserved by denaturation instead of digestion. Post-expansion labelling decrowds epitopes and reduces effective linkage error because the label's absolute size stays the same while the sample has grown, so its error shrinks by the expansion factor. RNA can also be anchored (ExFISH).

A key trade-off is signal: the fluorophore density drops by roughly the cube of the expansion factor, and some dyes are destroyed by the free-radical polymerisation, so bright labelling and efficient detection are essential.

Imaging is done on a confocal, spinning disk, light-sheet or SIM/STED, often with water-immersion or long working distance objectives because expanded samples are thick and mostly water.

tagline: Mapping the fluorescence lifetime, which depends on the fluorophore's environment but not on its concentration, turns a fluorescence image into a quantitative readout of FRET, metabolism and local chemistry.
principle: After excitation, a population of fluorophores decays to the ground state with rate k_r + k_nr, so fluorescence decays exponentially with lifetime τ = 1/(k_r + k_nr), typically 1-5 ns for common dyes and fluorescent proteins. Any process that adds a non-radiative pathway, such as FRET to an acceptor, collisional quenching, binding, or changes in viscosity, pH or ion concentration that alter the excited-state dynamics, shortens τ. Because τ is an intrinsic property of the excited state, it is largely independent of concentration, excitation intensity, path length and moderate photobleaching, which makes it more robust than intensity.

In the time domain the standard approach is time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC): a pulsed laser (picosecond diode, supercontinuum or femtosecond Ti:Sapphire at 20-80 MHz) excites the sample, and electronics record the delay between each laser pulse and the detected photon, building a histogram of arrival times per pixel. The measured decay is the true decay convolved with the instrument response function (IRF), so fitting by reconvolution or tail-fitting is used. Time-gated cameras and SPAD arrays offer widefield alternatives.

In the frequency domain the excitation is intensity-modulated at frequency ω (tens of MHz), and the emission is delayed in phase and reduced in modulation; for a single exponential, tan φ = ωτ and m = 1/√(1 + ω²τ²). Gated intensified cameras make this fast in widefield.

Phasor analysis avoids fitting by transforming each pixel's decay into two coordinates (g, s), the cosine and sine Fourier components at the laser repetition frequency. Single-exponential decays lie on a universal semicircle; mixtures of two species lie on a straight line between their positions, with position along the line proportional to the fractional contribution. This makes heterogeneous samples and FRET populations easy to visualise and segment.

Biological uses include FRET-FLIM (donor lifetime shortening), metabolic imaging using NAD(P)H (free ~0.4 ns vs protein-bound ~1-3+ ns) and FAD, lifetime-based biosensors (calcium, chloride, cAMP), molecular rotors for viscosity, and separating fluorophores with overlapping spectra but different lifetimes.

quiz.q: Why is FLIM preferred to intensity-based FRET in many cell experiments?
quiz.a: Donor lifetime is independent of donor concentration and of acceptor-donor stoichiometry in the measurement itself, and no correction for acceptor bleed-through or direct excitation is needed; one only needs a donor-only control.

quiz.q: What is the IRF and how do you measure it?
quiz.a: The instrument response function is the system's timing response to an infinitely short pulse: laser pulse width plus detector and electronics jitter. Measure it with a scattering sample or a very short-lifetime dye under the same settings, and convolve the model with it during fitting.

quiz.q: What is pile-up in TCSPC?
quiz.a: Electronics usually record only the first photon per cycle; at high count rates later photons are lost, so early arrivals are over-represented and lifetimes appear shorter. Keep rates below a few percent of the laser rate or use dead-time-corrected hardware.

quiz.q: How do phasor plots show a mixture of two species?
quiz.a: Each single-exponential species lies on the universal semicircle; a pixel containing both lies on the straight line connecting them, and its position along the line gives the fractional intensity contribution.

tagline: Non-radiative dipole-dipole energy transfer from a donor to an acceptor falls off with the sixth power of distance, making it a molecular ruler and interaction sensor over 1-10 nm.
principle: Förster resonance energy transfer occurs when an excited donor and a ground-state acceptor are close enough that their transition dipoles couple. Energy moves without emission of a photon at a rate k_T = (1/τ_D)(R0/r)⁶, which competes with the donor's other decay pathways. The efficiency is E = 1/(1 + (r/R0)⁶), where R0, the Förster radius, is the distance at which E = 50%. Because of the steep sixth-power dependence, FRET is sensitive mainly between about 0.5 R0 and 2 R0, i.e. roughly 2-10 nm.

R0 depends on the spectral overlap integral J between donor emission and acceptor absorption, the donor quantum yield Q_D, the refractive index n of the medium, and the orientation factor κ², which ranges from 0 to 4 and is taken as 2/3 for freely rotating dipoles. For typical pairs R0 is 4-6 nm.

In cells FRET is measured in several ways. Sensitized emission compares donor and acceptor channel intensities under donor excitation, and must correct for donor bleed-through into the acceptor channel and for direct excitation of the acceptor (three-cube methods). Acceptor photobleaching measures the donor's increase after destroying the acceptor. FLIM measures the donor lifetime shortening. Spectral and anisotropy (homo-FRET) methods also exist.

At the single-molecule level (smFRET), one donor and one acceptor on the same molecule report distances and conformational dynamics, with alternating laser excitation (ALEX) or pulsed interleaved excitation (PIE) to sort molecules by stoichiometry and remove donor-only or acceptor-only species. Correction factors for leakage, direct excitation and detection efficiency (γ) are required for accurate distances.

Genetically encoded FRET biosensors (calcium cameleons, kinase activity reporters) and intermolecular FRET between tagged proteins are the main uses in cell biology. A positive FRET signal implies proximity within ~10 nm, but the absence of FRET does not prove absence of interaction, because geometry or orientation may prevent transfer.
light_path: Excitation at the donor wavelength (and separately at the acceptor wavelength for corrections or ALEX) via filter cubes, lasers or a monochromator.
Emission split into donor and acceptor channels by a dichroic (image splitter or two cameras) or measured sequentially through filter sets.
For FLIM-FRET the donor emission is time-resolved with TCSPC; for smFRET confocal setups, photons go to two APDs with alternating laser excitation.
Control samples (donor-only, acceptor-only) are imaged with identical settings to derive correction coefficients.

limitations: Absolute distances require careful corrections and assumptions about κ².
Negative results are inconclusive.

Fluorescent protein pairs give modest dynamic range and may oligomerise.

Conformational dynamics of single proteins and nucleic acids (smFRET).

sample_prep: Use monomeric fluorescent proteins (e.g. A206K mutations) and bright, well-matched pairs (mTurquoise2-mVenus, mClover3-mRuby3, mNeonGreen-mScarlet). For acceptor photobleaching, bleach a region and use an unbleached region in the same cell as control for donor photobleaching and drift.
Use FLIM when stoichiometry varies or quantitation is important.
For smFRET use ALEX/PIE to compute stoichiometry S and filter molecules with exactly one donor and one acceptor.
pitfalls: Bleed-through of donor emission into the acceptor channel and direct excitation of the acceptor produce apparent FRET without interaction.
Bystander FRET from crowding at high concentration, especially in membranes, mimics specific interaction.
Acceptor photobleaching can photoconvert some acceptors (e.g. YFP variants) to donor-like species, or bleach the donor, biasing E.
κ² assumptions fail for rigidly attached dyes or FP barrels, so absolute distances become uncertain.
Incomplete acceptor maturation or labelling lowers apparent E.
Spectral changes of the acceptor with environment (pH, chloride for YFP) alter signals.

quiz.q: Write the FRET efficiency equation and explain what makes FRET a good ruler.
quiz.a: E = 1/(1+(r/R0)⁶). The sixth-power dependence means E changes from ~98% to ~2% between 0.5 R0 and 2 R0, so it is very sensitive to distance changes around R0, typically 5 nm.

quiz.q: What corrections are needed in sensitized-emission FRET?
quiz.a: Donor emission leaking into the acceptor channel (bleed-through), direct acceptor excitation at the donor wavelength, background, and ideally normalisation for expression and the detection-efficiency ratio. Coefficients come from donor-only and acceptor-only samples.

quiz.q: You see no FRET between two proteins thought to interact. Does that prove they do not?
quiz.a: No. Fluorophores may be more than 10 nm apart even in a complex, orientations may be unfavourable, labelling or maturation may be incomplete, or unlabelled endogenous protein may compete. Use positive controls and alternative tag positions.

quiz.q: How does κ² affect FRET-derived distances?
quiz.a: R0 ∝ κ^(1/3); using 2/3 assumes fast isotropic rotation. Anisotropy measurements can check rotational freedom; rigid dyes introduce uncertainty of tens of percent in distance.

tagline: Fluctuations of fluorescence from a sub-femtolitre volume, analysed by autocorrelation, give concentrations, diffusion coefficients and binding in solution and living cells.
principle: In fluorescence correlation spectroscopy a tightly focused laser defines a small observation volume (~0.2-1 fL). At nanomolar concentrations only a few molecules are inside at a time, so their entry, exit and photophysics produce intensity fluctuations whose relative size is large. The normalised autocorrelation G(τ) = ⟨δF(t)δF(t+τ)⟩/⟨F⟩² measures how long fluctuations persist.

For free 3D diffusion through a Gaussian volume with lateral radius ω0 and axial radius ωz, G(τ) has an amplitude 1/N (N = mean number of molecules in the volume) and decays on a diffusion time τ_D = ω0²/(4D). Fitting G(τ) therefore gives concentration and diffusion coefficient, after calibrating ω0 with a dye of known D. Fast photophysical processes (triplet, blinking, protonation) add an exponential term at µs times.

The brightness per molecule, counts per second divided by N, reports oligomerisation: a dimer of identical fluorophores is twice as bright. Photon counting histogram (PCH) and number-and-brightness (N&B) analyses exploit this further.

Dual-colour fluorescence cross-correlation spectroscopy (FCCS) correlates two spectrally distinct channels. Only molecules carrying both labels give cross-correlation, so the cross-correlation amplitude measures the concentration of complexes, a direct readout of binding in solution or in live cells. Imperfect overlap of the two foci and spectral cross-talk must be corrected.

Imaging variants extend FCS to many points: raster image correlation spectroscopy (RICS) uses the time structure of a confocal raster scan, while camera-based imaging FCS with TIRF or SPIM computes correlation curves for every pixel. STED-FCS shrinks the observation area to reveal nanoscale hindered diffusion in membranes, and the dependence of τ_D on spot size (FCS diffusion laws) distinguishes free, domain-confined and meshwork-hindered diffusion.
light_path: A stable continuous-wave or pulsed laser (488, 561, 640 nm) is expanded to overfill the back aperture of a high-NA water-immersion objective, producing a diffraction-limited focus.
The focus is parked at a chosen position in the sample (no scanning for point FCS).
Fluorescence passes a dichroic, a pinhole of about 1 Airy unit that defines the axial extent, and an emission filter.
Photons are detected by single-photon detectors (APD, hybrid PMT); for cross-correlation two detectors are used in different colours, or split 50:50 to remove afterpulsing.
A hardware or software correlator computes G(τ) from ~µs to seconds.

Take several short runs (e.g. 5-10 × 10 s) and discard runs with bleaching trends or bright aggregate spikes.

Refractive-index mismatch or wrong collar setting distorts the volume and biases D and N.

quiz.q: What two parameters does a simple FCS fit give and how do you convert them to physical quantities?
quiz.a: The amplitude G(0) = 1/N gives the mean number of molecules in the volume; with V_eff = π^(3/2)ω0²ωz this gives concentration. The decay time τ_D gives D = ω0²/(4τ_D). Both need ω0 and κ calibrated with a dye of known D.

quiz.q: Why must FCS be done at low concentrations?
quiz.a: The relative fluctuation amplitude scales as 1/N; at micromolar concentrations hundreds of molecules are in the volume and fluctuations become too small relative to noise.

quiz.q: How does FCCS measure binding and what limits it?
quiz.a: Only doubly labelled complexes fluctuate in both channels together, so cross-correlation amplitude is proportional to their concentration. Limits are imperfect overlap of the two foci (chromatic aberration), spectral cross-talk, incomplete labelling and unlabelled endogenous partners; positive and negative controls set the scale.

quiz.q: When would you choose FCS over FRAP?
quiz.a: FCS for low concentrations, fast diffusion (µs-ms), absolute concentrations and brightness, and binding by cross-correlation. FRAP for higher expression levels, slow exchange and immobile fractions over seconds to minutes.

tagline: Bleach (or photoactivate) the fluorescent molecules in a region and watch how fast and how completely the signal recovers (or spreads) to measure mobility, binding and exchange.
principle: In fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, a brief intense laser exposure irreversibly bleaches fluorophores in a defined region of interest. Unbleached molecules from the surroundings then move in, and the region's fluorescence recovers. The time course reports how molecules move (diffusion, flow) and how long they stay bound; the plateau reports the mobile fraction, while the unrecovered part is the immobile fraction on the time scale of the experiment.

For pure 2D diffusion into a uniformly bleached circular spot of radius w, Axelrod and Soumpasis derived closed-form recovery curves with characteristic time τ_D = w²/(4D). The recovery half-time scales with the square of the bleach radius, a useful check: if t½ is independent of spot size, recovery is limited by binding, not diffusion.

Many intracellular proteins recover by a combination of diffusion and binding. Sprague and colleagues showed that, depending on rates, FRAP falls into regimes: pure diffusion, effective diffusion (fast binding, D_eff reduced), reaction-dominant (diffusion fast compared with binding, recovery reflects k_off), or full reaction-diffusion. In the reaction-dominant regime recovery is approximately exponential with rate k_off, giving residence times directly.

Variants include FLIP (fluorescence loss in photobleaching: repeatedly bleach one region and watch loss elsewhere to test connectivity), inverse FRAP (bleach everything except a region), half-nucleus FRAP, line-FRAP for fast diffusers, and photoactivation or photoconversion (PA-GFP, Dendra2, mEos) where a region is switched on and the spreading of signal is followed, giving the inverse experiment with low background.

Data must be normalised for acquisition bleaching and for the total fluorescence lost in the bleach (double normalisation), and the bleach profile should be measured, because the effective bleached region is often larger than the nominal ROI due to diffusion during bleaching and the 3D shape of the focus.
light_path: A confocal (point-scanning or spinning disk with a FRAP module) images the cell at low laser power to record pre-bleach frames.
A galvanometer or dedicated photomanipulation scanner directs high-power laser light (same line as imaging, or 405 nm for photoactivation) to the ROI for a short bleach.
Imaging resumes immediately at low power and appropriate frame rate to follow recovery.
Intensities in the bleached ROI, a whole-cell reference ROI and a background ROI are extracted for normalisation and fitting.

resolution.z: Bleach volume extends through much of the cell thickness (axially elongated focus)

tips: Acquire enough pre-bleach frames to establish the baseline, and sample fast early in recovery (where the information is) and slower later.
Use several bleach sizes: diffusion-limited recovery scales with w², binding-limited does not.
Measure the actual post-bleach profile and use the effective radius in fitting.

Include a fixed-cell control to quantify reversible photobleaching and photoswitching.
Keep the bleached area small relative to the cell, or account for the finite pool.
pitfalls: Reversible photobleaching (dark-state recovery of EGFP, YFP) produces an apparent fast recovering mobile fraction even in fixed cells.

Cell or nuclear movement shifts the ROI and creates spurious recovery.

quiz.q: How would you tell whether a FRAP recovery is limited by diffusion or by binding?
quiz.a: Vary the bleach spot size: diffusion-limited recovery time scales with the square of the radius, binding-limited recovery is independent of it. Also compare with free GFP of similar size, and check whether recovery is spatially uniform (binding) or fills in from the edges (diffusion).

quiz.q: What normalisations do FRAP data need?
quiz.a: Background subtraction, correction for acquisition bleaching via a reference region, and correction for the fraction of total fluorescence removed by the bleach; this double normalisation avoids underestimating the mobile fraction.

quiz.q: Your fixed-cell control shows 15% recovery. What is happening?
quiz.a: Reversible photobleaching or photoswitching: some fluorophores entered dark states and spontaneously returned. Reduce bleach intensity, change FP, or subtract this component.

tagline: Localizing and linking the positions of individual molecules over time gives trajectories that reveal diffusion modes, confinement, binding and transport hidden in ensemble measurements.
principle: Single-particle tracking (SPT) has two steps: localization of each particle in each frame (as in SMLM, by fitting the PSF to nm precision), and linking of localizations into trajectories. Probes range from gold and latex beads and quantum dots (bright, large, potentially multivalent) to organic dyes on tags (HaloTag/SNAP with JF dyes) and photoactivatable fluorescent proteins in sptPALM, which allows thousands of short trajectories per cell at high density by activating only a few molecules at a time.

The mean squared displacement (MSD) as a function of lag time distinguishes motion types: linear for free diffusion (MSD = 2dDτ), sublinear and plateauing for confinement, sublinear power law for anomalous subdiffusion, and quadratic for directed motion. Localization error adds a positive offset (4σ² in 2D), and motion blur during finite exposure subtracts a term, so a fit must include both.

Because individual trajectories are short (photobleaching), analysis often pools displacements: the distribution of jump distances for a given lag time is a sum of Rayleigh-like components for each diffusive population, enabling estimation of bound and free fractions (as in Spot-On). Hidden Markov models (e.g. vbSPT) infer states and transition rates. Residence times of chromatin-bound factors are measured with long exposures that blur fast molecules and keep only immobile ones, corrected for photobleaching.

Linking is a combinatorial problem: as particle density rises relative to typical displacements per frame, assignments become ambiguous. Approaches range from nearest-neighbour to global optimisation with linear assignment (u-track, TrackMate's LAP tracker) including gap closing for blinking and merging/splitting events, to multiple hypothesis tracking. A useful rule is that the typical displacement between frames should be much smaller than the mean nearest-neighbour distance.

Interpretation needs care because measured trajectories are biased: fast molecules leave the focal plane (out-of-focus loss), are blurred and missed, and yield shorter tracks; immobile ones are over-represented. Simulations with the same imaging parameters are a standard control.
light_path: Lasers for excitation (and 405 nm for photoactivation in sptPALM) are delivered in TIRF or HILO geometry, or light-sheet for deep nuclear tracking.
Stroboscopic illumination (short pulses within each frame) is used to reduce motion blur of fast particles.
A high-NA objective collects fluorescence onto an EMCCD or sCMOS camera at frame rates of ~10-1000 Hz.
Software detects and localizes spots, links them into tracks with a motion model, and computes MSD, jump-distance distributions or state models.

Quantum dots and gold allow very long or very fast tracking.
limitations: Short tracks due to photobleaching limit per-trajectory statistics.
Biases from motion blur, out-of-focus loss and linking errors.
Large probes (QDs, beads) can perturb motion and crosslink targets.
Requires sparse labelling and careful analysis.

Synaptic receptor exchange between synaptic and extrasynaptic sites.

tips: Set exposure and frame interval so that displacements per frame are well below the nearest-neighbour distance; reduce density by lowering activation or labelling.
Use stroboscopic illumination for fast molecules to minimise motion blur.
Measure σ from immobile molecules or the MSD intercept and include it in fits.
Fit D from the first few MSD points only, and use jump-distance or HMM approaches for multi-state data.
Correct residence time distributions for photobleaching using an immobile reference and vary frame interval to check consistency.
Validate the full pipeline on simulated trajectories with the same density, σ and blur.
pitfalls: Motion blur: fast particles are smeared, localized poorly or missed, biasing towards slow populations and underestimating the free fraction.
Linking errors at high density create spurious long jumps and artificial fast components or mixed trajectories.
Out-of-focus loss: fast molecules leave the focal plane, shortening tracks and biasing fractions; correct for axial detection range.
Over-interpreting anomalous exponents from short tracks, where noise and localization error produce apparent subdiffusion.
Multivalent probes (quantum dots, IgG) crosslink targets and slow them.
Photobleaching truncates residence-time measurements.

quiz.q: Why does the MSD not pass through the origin?
quiz.a: Localization error adds a positive offset 4σ² (in 2D), while motion blur during finite exposure subtracts a term proportional to D·t_E. The intercept therefore reflects both, and can be negative for fast particles.

quiz.q: How do you choose frame rate and density for sptPALM?
quiz.a: The displacement per frame (√(4DΔt)) should be much smaller than the mean distance between simultaneously visible molecules to avoid linking errors, and exposures short enough to limit blur; activation is tuned to keep density low, often well below 1 molecule per µm² per frame.

quiz.q: How would you measure the bound fraction of a transcription factor?
quiz.a: Fast (~100-200 Hz) stroboscopic SPT, then fit jump-distance distributions with a two- or three-state model that corrects for out-of-focus loss (e.g. Spot-On), validated against H2B (bound) and free Halo controls; residence times from long-exposure imaging corrected for bleaching.

quiz.q: What does an MSD exponent α < 1 tell you?
quiz.a: Subdiffusion, which can come from crowding, binding, confinement or a fractal environment, but short tracks and localization error also bias α downward, so it should be checked with simulations and longer trajectories.

tagline: Recording a full emission spectrum at every pixel lets you separate fluorophores, and autofluorescence, whose colours overlap too much for filters.
principle: Conventional multicolour imaging assumes each channel sees only one fluorophore. With more labels, or with broad autofluorescence, emission spectra overlap and each channel contains a mixture. Spectral imaging records many narrow wavelength bands per pixel (a lambda stack or hyperspectral cube), so each pixel has a measured spectrum.

Linear unmixing models the pixel spectrum as a weighted sum of reference spectra (endmembers), S(λ) = Σ a_i R_i(λ) + noise, and solves for the abundances a_i by least squares, usually with a non-negativity constraint. This requires at least as many spectral channels as components and reference spectra recorded under identical conditions. The separability depends on how different the spectra are; nearly identical spectra give an ill-conditioned problem in which noise is amplified.

Hardware includes confocal detectors with a prism or grating dispersing light onto a multichannel GaAsP or PMT array (e.g. 32 channels at ~9 nm), adjustable slit detectors, tunable filters (liquid crystal or acousto-optic) on widefield systems, image-mapping or snapshot spectrometers, and excitation-scanning approaches in which the excitation wavelength is varied instead (excitation fingerprinting). Flow cytometry and imaging mass-cytometry use analogous unmixing.

Spectral phasors provide a fit-free alternative: the Fourier sine and cosine components of each pixel's spectrum map it to a point; mixtures fall on lines between pure species, which helps identify unknown components and segment images. Valm et al used spectral imaging and unmixing to separate six organelle labels simultaneously in live cells.

Spectral imaging also enables label-free work: autofluorescence spectra (flavins, lipofuscin, chlorophyll) can be unmixed as separate channels and removed from the labels of interest, which is crucial in plant tissues and aged neuronal tissue.
light_path: Excitation by one or more laser lines (confocal) or broadband source with tunable filter (widefield).
Emission passes a main beam splitter, then a dispersive element (prism or grating) spreads the spectrum across a linear detector array, or a tunable filter selects bands sequentially.
Signal is recorded as a lambda stack (x, y, λ) per frame.
Reference spectra are acquired from single-labelled samples or selected regions with the same settings.
Software performs linear unmixing or phasor analysis to produce abundance images for each component.

resolution.z: As for the underlying microscope

strengths: Separates fluorophores with strongly overlapping spectra.
Removes autofluorescence as an explicit component.
Increases multiplexing on a single excitation.
Can detect unexpected spectral changes (e.g. environment-sensitive dyes).
limitations: Lower SNR per channel and slower acquisition.
Requires accurate reference spectra.
Similar spectra amplify noise and cross-talk.
Saturation or nonlinearity invalidates the linear model.
best_for: Highly multiplexed fixed and live imaging (many organelles or cell types).
Tissues and plants with strong autofluorescence.
Separating GFP from YFP or other close pairs.
Spectral FRET and environment-sensitive probes.
sample_prep: Prepare single-labelled controls for every fluorophore, plus an unlabelled sample for autofluorescence, mounted and imaged exactly as the experimental sample. Choose fluorophores with distinct spectral shapes and similar brightness, since a dim label next to a bright overlapping one is hard to recover.
tips: Record reference spectra on the same instrument, settings and sample environment (pH, mounting medium, fixation).
Avoid saturating any channel; saturation breaks the linear model.
Inspect residual images after unmixing to detect missing components.
Balance excitation powers so that labels contribute comparable signals.
Use spectral phasor plots to discover unknown components before choosing references.

Unaccounted autofluorescence is distributed into label channels.
Negative abundance values or speckled noise where spectra are too similar.
Spectral shifts from FRET or binding change effective spectra and bias unmixing.
Channel-dependent detector gain or offset differences distort spectra.

quiz.q: Explain linear unmixing and its requirements.
quiz.a: Each pixel spectrum is modelled as a non-negative weighted sum of reference spectra and solved by least squares. It needs at least as many channels as components, accurate references recorded under identical conditions, no saturation and sufficiently distinct spectra.

quiz.q: How do you validate an unmixed image?
quiz.a: Unmix single-labelled controls and check that signal appears only in the correct channel; inspect residuals; use unlabelled samples for autofluorescence; confirm key findings with sequential excitation or alternative labels.

quiz.q: Why does unmixing amplify noise?
quiz.a: When reference spectra are similar, the matrix RᵀR is ill-conditioned, so small noise in the measured spectrum produces large changes in the estimated abundances.

tagline: A tiny fraction of scattered light shifts in energy by molecular vibrations, giving a label-free chemical fingerprint of lipids, proteins, nucleic acids and metabolites.
principle: When light scatters from a molecule, almost all of it is elastically (Rayleigh) scattered at the incident frequency. A fraction of order 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁸ is inelastically scattered: the molecule ends in a different vibrational level, so the scattered photon loses (Stokes) or gains (anti-Stokes) the vibrational energy. The frequency shift, expressed in wavenumbers (cm⁻¹), is independent of the excitation wavelength and specific to chemical bonds, so the spectrum is a fingerprint of the sample's composition.

A vibration is Raman active if it changes the molecular polarizability. Intensity scales with the number of molecules, the square of the polarizability derivative and roughly the fourth power of the scattered frequency, so shorter excitation wavelengths give more signal but also more fluorescence background, which can swamp the weak Raman bands. Near-infrared excitation (785 nm, 1064 nm) reduces fluorescence and photodamage at the cost of signal.

Biological spectra have characteristic regions: the fingerprint region (~600-1800 cm⁻¹) with phenylalanine at 1003 cm⁻¹, amide I at ~1655 cm⁻¹, CH2 deformation at ~1440-1450 cm⁻¹, nucleic acid backbone and ring modes ~785 cm⁻¹; the cell-silent region (~1800-2700 cm⁻¹) where alkyne and carbon-deuterium tags appear without background; and the high-wavenumber C-H stretch region (~2800-3050 cm⁻¹), dominated by lipids (~2850) and proteins (~2930).

In confocal Raman microscopy a laser is focused to a diffraction-limited spot and the scattered light passes a pinhole and a spectrometer onto a cooled CCD; images are built by scanning, with one full spectrum per pixel, then analysed by multivariate methods (PCA, cluster analysis, non-negative matrix factorisation). Because cross-sections are tiny (~10⁻³⁰ to 10⁻²⁹ cm² vs ~10⁻¹⁶ cm² for fluorophore absorption), integration times of 0.1-1 s per pixel are typical, making whole-cell maps take minutes to hours.

Signal enhancements include resonance Raman (excitation tuned to an electronic absorption, as for cytochromes and carotenoids), surface-enhanced Raman (SERS, 10⁶-10¹⁰ enhancement near plasmonic metal nanostructures) and tip-enhanced Raman (TERS). Coherent Raman methods (CARS, SRS) amplify signals for fast imaging.
light_path: A narrow-linewidth laser (532, 633, 785 or 1064 nm) passes a laser-line clean-up filter.
A dichroic or edge filter reflects it into a high-NA objective focused on the sample, often on a CaF2 or quartz substrate.
Backscattered light is collected, the Rayleigh line removed by a notch or long-pass edge filter (blocking ~OD 6).
A confocal pinhole or fibre limits the collection volume.
A grating spectrometer disperses light onto a cooled, back-illuminated CCD.
The stage or beam is raster-scanned, recording a spectrum at each pixel; spectra are preprocessed and analysed.

resolution.z: ~1-2 µm confocal

equations.name: Raman shift
equations.meaning: Converts measured wavelength to vibrational energy, independent of excitation wavelength.

equations.name: Intensity scaling
equations.meaning: Linear in concentration and laser power, fourth power of scattered frequency, and the polarizability derivative.

equations.name: Anti-Stokes/Stokes ratio
equations.meaning: Boltzmann population of excited vibrational levels; can measure temperature.

strengths: Label-free chemical specificity.
Works on living or fixed cells and tissues without staining.
Narrow bands allow multiplexing with Raman tags.
Quantitative (linear in concentration).
limitations: Very weak signal; slow imaging.
Fluorescence background can overwhelm spectra.
Complex spectra require multivariate analysis and careful preprocessing.
Laser heating and photodamage at visible wavelengths.
best_for: Cell and tissue biochemistry without labels (lipids, proteins, nucleic acids).
Clinical tissue diagnostics and cell phenotyping.
Metabolic labelling with deuterium or alkyne tags.
Materials and pharmaceutical analysis, microplastics, bacteria identification.
sample_prep: Use Raman-quiet substrates such as CaF2, quartz or aluminium-coated slides, since glass and plastics contribute strong backgrounds. Live cells can be imaged in buffer with water-dipping objectives; fixation (formalin) changes some spectral features and should be consistent across samples. Avoid fluorescent stains and mounting media.
tips: Calibrate wavenumber with a silicon wafer (520.7 cm⁻¹) and a standard such as polystyrene or neon lines each day.
Choose 785 nm excitation for tissues with high autofluorescence; 532 nm for higher signal in thin, weakly fluorescent samples.
Remove cosmic rays, subtract background and normalise consistently; apply the same pipeline to all groups.
Collect spectra from substrate and medium to subtract their contributions.
Keep power and exposure below damage thresholds; check spectra for burning (growth of broad carbon bands near 1350 and 1580 cm⁻¹).
pitfalls: Fluorescence background rising across the spectrum hides bands; overly aggressive baseline correction can create or remove features.
Photodamage and heating alter the sample during measurement.
Substrate and medium bands misattributed to the sample.
Overfitting classifiers on small sample numbers; batch effects between days.
Cosmic-ray spikes mistaken for sharp bands.

quiz.q: Why is Raman scattering so weak and how is it enhanced?
quiz.a: It is a second-order process with cross-sections ~10⁻³⁰ cm², about 10¹⁴ times weaker than fluorescence absorption. Enhancement comes from resonance (tuning to an electronic transition), plasmonic fields (SERS, TERS) or coherent driving (CARS, SRS).

quiz.q: How do you choose an excitation wavelength?
quiz.a: Shorter wavelengths give more signal (ν⁴) and better resolution but more fluorescence and photodamage; 785 nm is a common compromise for biological tissue, 532 nm for thin weakly fluorescent samples, 1064 nm for highly fluorescent ones.

quiz.q: What is the cell-silent region used for?
quiz.a: Between about 1800 and 2700 cm⁻¹ cells have almost no endogenous bands, so alkyne, nitrile or carbon-deuterium labels show up background-free, enabling metabolic imaging of e.g. deuterated glucose, fatty acids or EdU.

tagline: Two synchronised pulsed lasers whose frequency difference matches a molecular vibration drive it coherently, amplifying Raman signals by orders of magnitude for video-rate label-free chemical imaging.
principle: Coherent Raman scattering uses a pump beam at ω_p and a Stokes beam at ω_S. When ω_p − ω_S equals a vibrational frequency Ω, the beat between the fields drives the molecules' vibrations in phase across the focus. This coherent excitation gives signals many orders of magnitude stronger than spontaneous Raman, enabling pixel dwell times of µs and video-rate imaging. Because the processes are nonlinear (third order), signal arises only at the focus, giving intrinsic 3D sectioning as in multiphoton microscopy.

In coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS), the vibrational coherence scatters a further pump photon to a new frequency ω_as = 2ω_p − ω_S, blue-shifted from both lasers and from fluorescence. The signal is proportional to |χ⁽³⁾|² I_p² I_S. χ⁽³⁾ includes a resonant Raman part and a non-resonant electronic part that is always present, so CARS has a non-resonant background, dispersive (distorted) lineshapes and a signal quadratic in concentration. CARS is very strong for dense C-H vibrations such as lipids.

In stimulated Raman scattering (SRS), energy is transferred from the pump to the Stokes field: the pump loses intensity (stimulated Raman loss, SRL) and the Stokes gains (stimulated Raman gain, SRG). The fractional change, typically 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁷, is proportional to Im χ⁽³⁾_R, the concentration and the other beam intensity. To detect such small changes, one beam is modulated at MHz frequencies and a lock-in amplifier detects the transferred modulation on the other beam, at frequencies where laser noise is near shot-noise limited. SRS is free of non-resonant background, has spontaneous-Raman-like spectra and is linear in concentration, which makes quantitative imaging straightforward.

Picosecond lasers (~2-7 ps, ~2-10 cm⁻¹ bandwidth) address a single Raman band; hyperspectral SRS is done by tuning the laser, or with chirped femtosecond pulses (spectral focusing), where the time delay selects the Raman shift. Typical sources are an optical parametric oscillator pumped by a ~1031-1064 nm laser, which also serves as Stokes beam.

Raman tags expand SRS beyond endogenous contrast: alkynes, nitriles and carbon-deuterium bonds in the cell-silent region report metabolism (e.g. deuterated water, glucose, EdU), and electronic pre-resonance SRS with specially designed dyes reaches near-µM sensitivity and dozens of resolvable colours. Stimulated Raman histology provides rapid intraoperative tissue imaging.
light_path: A picosecond or femtosecond laser system provides two synchronised pulse trains: a tunable pump (OPO output, e.g. 700-1000 nm) and a Stokes beam (e.g. 1031 or 1064 nm).
For SRS, one beam passes an electro-optic or acousto-optic modulator at ~10-20 MHz.
The beams are combined on a dichroic with a delay stage for temporal overlap and steered into a laser scanning microscope.
A high-NA objective focuses both beams; signals are generated only in the focal volume.
For SRS, a high-NA condenser collects the transmitted beams, a filter blocks the modulated beam and a large-area photodiode detects the other; a lock-in amplifier extracts the modulation transfer.
For CARS, the blue-shifted anti-Stokes light is filtered and detected by PMT in forward or epi direction.

resolution.why: Nonlinear dependence on both beams confines signal to the focus, similar to two-photon microscopy with near-infrared light; sensitivity, not resolution, is usually the limiting factor.

Intrinsic optical sectioning and deep imaging with near-IR light.
SRS gives quantitative, background-free, Raman-like spectra.
Small Raman tags (alkyne, deuterium) minimally perturb biology and allow multiplexing.
limitations: Expensive and complex dual-laser systems needing temporal and spatial overlap.
Lower sensitivity than fluorescence.
CARS has non-resonant background and nonlinear concentration dependence.

sample_prep: Live or fixed cells and tissues can be imaged without staining. Use thin coverslips and a high-NA condenser for transmitted SRS detection; for thick tissue use epi-detection. tips: Optimise temporal overlap on a strong sample (e.g. oil or polystyrene beads) each session.
Always acquire an off-resonance image (shifted by ~50-100 cm⁻¹) to reveal non-Raman background in SRS and non-resonant background in CARS.
Keep combined power at the sample within safe limits (often tens of mW per beam) to avoid photodamage.
Use spectral unmixing of lipid and protein channels from two or more Raman shifts.
Balance photodiode saturation with the modulation detection range; use reverse-biased large-area photodiodes.
pitfalls: CARS non-resonant background gives contrast where no resonant species exist and distorts spectra.
In SRS, transient absorption and two-photon absorption by pigments (haemoglobin, melanin) and cross-phase modulation produce signals that mimic Raman contrast; check off-resonance.
Photodamage from high peak powers, especially at shorter pump wavelengths.
Drift of temporal overlap with temperature changes alters signals during long sessions.

quiz.q: Why is SRS generally preferred over CARS for quantitative imaging?
quiz.a: SRS is free of the non-resonant background, has undistorted Raman lineshapes matching spontaneous Raman spectra, and its signal is linear in concentration; CARS signals depend quadratically on concentration and interfere with non-resonant background.

quiz.q: How is a 10⁻⁶ intensity change detected in SRS?
quiz.a: By modulating one beam at MHz frequencies, where laser intensity noise approaches the shot-noise limit, and using lock-in detection of the modulation transferred to the other beam.

quiz.q: How do you confirm an SRS signal is truly Raman?
quiz.a: Tune off-resonance: true Raman contrast disappears, whereas pump-probe artefacts such as two-photon absorption or cross-phase modulation persist. Also check the spectrum with hyperspectral SRS.

tagline: Intense pulsed light is converted to exactly twice (or three times) its frequency by ordered non-centrosymmetric structures (SHG) or by interfaces (THG), giving label-free images of collagen, muscle, microtubules and lipid boundaries.
principle: In strong optical fields the induced polarization of a material is not linear in the field: P = ε0[χ⁽¹⁾E + χ⁽²⁾E² + χ⁽³⁾E³ + ...]. The second-order term radiates at twice the incident frequency, which is second harmonic generation (SHG); the third-order term gives third harmonic generation (THG). Unlike two-photon fluorescence, harmonic generation involves only virtual states: no energy is absorbed, the signal is emitted instantaneously, there is no lifetime and no photobleaching of the contrast mechanism.

χ⁽²⁾ vanishes in any medium with inversion symmetry, so SHG requires molecular non-centrosymmetry and, because the emission is coherent, that the emitters are also arranged with consistent polar order over a sizeable fraction of the wavelength. Fibrillar collagen (types I and II), myosin in muscle A-bands, polarly aligned microtubule arrays (axons, mitotic spindles), cellulose and starch meet this requirement. Randomly oriented molecules cancel. Because emission adds coherently, SHG intensity scales with the square of the number of aligned emitters in the focus as well as with the square of the excitation intensity.

Coherence also makes SHG directional. Phase matching favours forward emission, and the forward-to-backward ratio depends on fibril diameter, packing and spacing; backward signal in tissue also comes from forward light backscattered by the sample. Comparing forward and backward channels, and using polarization-resolved SHG to measure χ⁽²⁾ tensor ratios and fibre orientation, gives information about collagen organisation, used for example in tumour-associated collagen signatures and fibrosis scoring.

THG is allowed in all media but, for a tightly focused beam in a homogeneous medium, contributions on either side of the focus cancel because of the Gouy phase shift. A signal therefore arises only where χ⁽³⁾ or refractive index changes within the focus: interfaces, lipid droplets, membranes, myelin and mineralised structures. THG is useful for label-free morphology in embryos and tissue.

Harmonic generation is commonly added to multiphoton microscopes: a femtosecond laser at 800-1050 nm gives SHG at 400-525 nm, while 1200-1300 nm (OPO or fibre lasers) gives SHG at 600-650 and THG at 400-433 nm. Membrane-potential imaging with SHG dyes inserted asymmetrically into one membrane leaflet is a specialised application.
light_path: A femtosecond pulsed laser (Ti:Sapphire 800-1050 nm, or OPO/fibre laser 1200-1300 nm) with polarization control (half- and quarter-wave plates) enters a scanning microscope.
Galvanometer scanners raster the focus; a high-NA objective focuses into the sample.
Forward harmonic light is collected by a high-NA condenser, passes a narrow bandpass filter centred at λ/2 (or λ/3) and is detected by a PMT.
Backward (epi) harmonic light returns through the objective, is separated by a dichroic and filtered before a non-descanned PMT.
Two-photon fluorescence can be collected simultaneously in other channels.
