strengths: Label-free, specific contrast for collagen, myosin and polar microtubule arrays.
No photobleaching of the contrast mechanism; minimal photodamage at near-IR wavelengths.
Deep tissue imaging with intrinsic sectioning.
Polarization and F/B ratios report sub-resolution structural organisation.
limitations: Restricted to specific ordered structures (SHG) or interfaces (THG).
Forward detection needs transmission geometry; epi signals are weaker and mixed with backscattered forward light.
Signal depends on fibre orientation relative to laser polarization.
Requires femtosecond lasers.
best_for: Collagen architecture in tumours, fibrosis, cartilage, tendon and skin.
Sarcomere structure and muscle contraction.
Morphology of developing embryos (THG of lipid and cell boundaries).
Combining with two-photon autofluorescence for label-free tissue histology.
sample_prep: Fresh, fixed or cleared tissues and live animals can be imaged without labels. For forward detection, use thin sections or explants on coverslips with a condenser of high NA. Avoid embedding methods that disrupt collagen structure; note that some clearing and dehydration protocols alter SHG intensity.
tips: Use narrow bandpass filters centred exactly at λ/2 to exclude two-photon autofluorescence.
Use circular polarization to image fibres of all orientations equally, or acquire a series of linear polarizations for polarization-resolved SHG.
Record forward and backward channels together and keep detector gains fixed for comparing F/B ratios.
Confirm SHG by tuning the laser: the signal wavelength must follow exactly half the excitation wavelength, and it has no lifetime in FLIM.
Correct for depth-dependent attenuation when comparing intensities.
pitfalls: Two-photon autofluorescence leaking into the SHG channel, especially with wide filters.
Orientation-dependent intensity misread as differences in collagen amount.
Comparing forward and backward signals from different thickness samples, which changes F/B ratios independent of structure.
Assuming THG contrast is specific to a molecule; it reports interfaces and index changes.

quiz.q: Why does SHG need non-centrosymmetric order?
quiz.a: In a centrosymmetric medium reversing the field must reverse the polarization, which forces χ⁽²⁾ = 0. In addition, the emitters must be polarly aligned over a sizeable fraction of the focal volume so their coherent contributions add rather than cancel.

quiz.q: How do you distinguish SHG from two-photon autofluorescence?
quiz.a: SHG appears at exactly half the excitation wavelength with a narrow bandwidth, shifts when the laser is tuned, shows no fluorescence lifetime and is strongly polarization- and direction-dependent.

quiz.q: Why is THG generated at interfaces?
quiz.a: In a homogeneous medium the Gouy phase shift across the focus causes THG generated before and after the focus to interfere destructively; a change in χ⁽³⁾ or refractive index breaks this cancellation.

tagline: Interferometric or computational measurement of the optical path delay through transparent cells gives quantitative phase maps, dry mass and, from many angles, 3D refractive-index tomograms without labels.
principle: Transparent cells barely absorb light but delay it, because their refractive index (~1.36-1.39) exceeds that of the medium (~1.335). The phase delay is φ = (2π/λ) ∫ (n − n_m) dz, the optical path difference in wavelengths. Phase contrast and DIC convert phase into intensity qualitatively; quantitative phase imaging (QPI) measures φ in radians at each pixel.

Interferometric methods combine the sample wave with a reference. In off-axis digital holographic microscopy (DHM) the reference is tilted, producing carrier fringes; the complex field is recovered by Fourier filtering a sideband, from a single frame, so imaging is fast and the field can be numerically refocused. Phase-shifting interferometry acquires several frames with stepped reference phases. Common-path designs (diffraction phase microscopy, SLIM based on a phase-contrast microscope with a spatial light modulator) are very stable. Non-interferometric methods include the transport-of-intensity equation, which infers phase from defocused intensity images, and Fourier ptychography, which synthesises a large-aperture complex image from many illumination angles.

Because the refractive index of biological solutions increases linearly with the concentration of dry matter (refractive increment α ≈ 0.18-0.21 mL/g for proteins), the integrated phase of a cell gives its dry mass, independent of shape and water content. This is used to measure cell growth rates with fg-pg precision.

A 2D phase map couples thickness and refractive index. Holotomography (optical diffraction tomography) separates them: the sample is illuminated from many angles (or rotated), each complex field is recorded, and the Fourier diffraction theorem maps each measurement onto a spherical cap (Ewald sphere) in 3D frequency space; under the Born or Rytov approximation this yields the 3D refractive-index distribution. As in widefield, a missing cone of axial frequencies causes axial elongation and index underestimation, partly corrected by regularised reconstructions.

QPI is label-free, gentle (low-intensity illumination) and quantitative, which makes it attractive for long-term live imaging, cell growth and drug response, but it lacks molecular specificity; it is increasingly combined with fluorescence or machine learning for organelle identification.
light_path: A low-coherence or laser source (often 520-650 nm) is split into sample and reference arms (or uses a common-path geometry).
The sample is illuminated by a plane wave; in holotomography, a galvanometer mirror or DMD scans the illumination angle.
The objective collects the transmitted field; the reference wave is recombined at a small angle (off-axis) or with phase steps.
A camera records the interferogram (hologram).
Software extracts the complex field (Fourier filtering), unwraps phase, removes background aberrations and, for tomography, reconstructs 3D refractive index.

resolution.xy: ~200-300 nm (QPI); ~110-200 nm (holotomography with synthetic aperture)

resolution.why: Coherent imaging resolution is set by the objective and illumination NA; holotomography combines angles to extend the aperture but has a missing cone axially.

equations.name: Phase delay
equations.formula: φ(x, y) = (2π/λ) ∫ [n(x, y, z) − n_m] dz = (2π/λ) · h · Δn
equations.meaning: Optical path difference through the cell; couples thickness h and index difference Δn.

equations.name: Dry mass density
equations.formula: σ(x, y) = λ φ(x, y) / (2π α)
equations.meaning: Mass per area from phase; α = refractive increment (~0.18-0.21 mL/g).

equations.name: Total dry mass
equations.meaning: Integrated phase gives cell dry mass.

equations.name: Hologram
equations.meaning: Off-axis interference; the carrier k_c separates the cross term in Fourier space.

equations.name: Fourier diffraction theorem
equations.formula: F[scattered field](k) ↔ F[scattering potential] on an Ewald sphere cap
equations.meaning: Each illumination angle samples a different spherical cap of the object's 3D spectrum.

key_numbers.value: ~mrad; sub-nm optical path stability in common-path systems

strengths: Label-free and quantitative (phase, dry mass, refractive index).
Low light dose, suitable for very long time lapses.
Fast single-shot acquisition (off-axis) and numerical refocusing.
3D refractive-index maps reveal organelles like lipid droplets and nucleoli.
limitations: No molecular specificity.
Phase wrapping for thick or high-index objects.
Multiple scattering breaks Born/Rytov approximations in thick tissue.
Coherent noise and missing cone artefacts.
best_for: Cell growth, mass accumulation and cell cycle studies.
Long-term label-free live-cell monitoring and drug screening.
Red blood cell morphology and membrane fluctuations.
Lipid droplet and organelle dynamics in 3D without labels.
sample_prep: Image cells in thin chambers or dishes with flat, clean glass bottoms and a well-defined medium (record its refractive index). Avoid phenol red if combining with fluorescence and ensure medium height is constant (the meniscus causes phase gradients). No staining is needed; for dry mass measurements avoid bubbles and debris, which create spurious phase.
tips: Acquire a background (cell-free) hologram to subtract system aberrations and parasitic fringes.
Use partially coherent illumination or temporal averaging to suppress speckle.
Choose a wavelength and sample thickness that keep phase below ~2π where possible, or use robust unwrapping.
Stabilise temperature, since index of medium and optical path drift with temperature.
Validate refractive index with beads of known index (e.g. polystyrene or silica) in the same medium.
pitfalls: Phase unwrapping errors produce sudden 2π jumps that look like structures.
Parasitic interference fringes from optics or dust add background patterns.
Mis-assuming refractive increment for lipids or nucleic acids (they differ from protein) biases dry mass.
Missing cone causes axial elongation and underestimated index in tomography.
Medium meniscus or evaporation changes background phase over time.

quiz.q: How do you get cell dry mass from a phase image?
quiz.a: Phase is proportional to the integral of refractive index excess, which is linearly proportional to dry-matter concentration with refractive increment α. Integrating phase over the cell and multiplying by λ/(2πα) gives dry mass, independent of shape and water content.

quiz.q: What does holotomography add over 2D QPI?
quiz.a: 2D phase couples thickness and index. Illuminating from many angles and inverting via the Fourier diffraction theorem gives the 3D refractive index distribution, separating thickness and index.

quiz.q: What limits QPI accuracy?
quiz.a: Coherent noise and parasitic fringes, phase unwrapping errors, temperature drift, multiple scattering in thick samples, the missing cone in tomography, and assumptions about refractive increment.

tagline: Interfering the weak light scattered by a nanoparticle or single protein with a strong reference reflection makes the signal scale with particle volume rather than volume squared, allowing label-free detection of single proteins and mass measurement.
principle: A particle much smaller than the wavelength scatters light with an amplitude proportional to its polarizability, which scales with its volume (d³), so scattered intensity falls as d⁶. For a single protein this is hopelessly small next to background. Interferometric scattering (iSCAT) detects the field instead: the scattered field E_s interferes with a reference field E_r, typically the light reflected at the glass-water interface of the coverslip. The detected intensity contains a cross term 2|E_r||E_s|cos φ that is linear in the scattered field, so the contrast scales with d³ (proportional to mass) instead of d⁶.

The reference reflection is weak (~0.4% at glass-water), which acts like an attenuator, increasing the relative interference contrast. The fundamental limit is shot noise: detecting a contrast c requires collecting about 1/c² photons per diffraction-limited spot, so very high photon fluxes, cameras with large full-well capacity and frame averaging are needed. Static scattering from coverslip roughness is much larger than the protein signal, so iSCAT relies on differential (ratiometric) imaging that removes the static background and highlights changes, such as a molecule landing.

The phase φ depends on the axial position of the particle relative to the focus and the reference, so contrast can change sign as a particle moves in z. For molecules landing on the coverslip surface, contrast is reproducible and proportional to mass. This is mass photometry: counting landing events and building a mass histogram reveals oligomeric states and complex stoichiometry in solution at nanomolar concentrations without labels, with mass accuracy of a few percent.

With gold nanoparticle labels (5-40 nm), iSCAT tracks single molecules with nm precision at µs time resolution and essentially unlimited observation time, since there is no photobleaching. This has been used to follow lipid diffusion, viruses, and the stepping of motor proteins. Label-free iSCAT can also image dynamic processes like microtubule polymerisation and membrane remodelling.
light_path: A stable, low-noise laser (e.g. 445-635 nm) is scanned or widely illuminates the sample through a high-NA oil objective; acousto-optic deflectors can scan the beam rapidly to average out speckle.
Light reflected at the coverslip-water interface (reference) and light scattered back by particles (signal) are collected by the same objective.
A polarizing beam splitter and quarter-wave plate separate the returning light from the illumination.

Light is imaged onto a high-full-well CMOS camera at high frame rates; a partial reflector or spatial mask in the Fourier plane may attenuate the reference to increase contrast (as in many mass photometers).
Frames are averaged and divided by preceding frames (ratiometric processing) to remove static background and reveal landing or moving particles.

resolution.xy: Diffraction-limited (~200-250 nm); localization precision ~nm with gold labels
resolution.z: Not depth-resolved by default; contrast depends on axial position
resolution.why: Imaging is diffraction-limited; detection sensitivity is limited by shot noise and residual background, and localization precision by photons.

equations.name: Detected intensity
equations.meaning: r = reference reflectivity amplitude, s = scattering amplitude, φ = phase difference; for small particles the cross term dominates over |s|².

equations.name: Interferometric contrast
equations.meaning: Linear in scattering amplitude, hence in particle volume or mass.

equations.name: Polarizability scaling
equations.meaning: Why interferometric detection outperforms dark-field for tiny particles.

equations.name: Shot-noise requirement
equations.meaning: Very small contrasts need very high photon fluxes and averaging.

strengths: Label-free single-molecule detection and mass measurement in solution.
No photobleaching; very long and very fast tracking with gold labels.
Small sample volumes, fast measurements (minutes).

limitations: No molecular specificity without labels.
Requires extremely stable, low-noise optics and very clean coverslips.
Contrast depends on refractive increment, so lipid-, sugar- or nucleic-acid-rich particles need different calibration.
Detection limited to near the coverslip surface; complex backgrounds in cells.
best_for: Oligomeric state, complex assembly and binding stoichiometry of purified proteins (mass photometry).
Fast nm tracking of gold-labelled membrane proteins, lipids and motors.

sample_prep: Use very clean coverslips (sonicated and rinsed, sometimes plasma cleaned) and filtered buffers; detergent micelles, lipid vesicles and aggregates in the buffer create landing events. For mass photometry dilute protein to ~5-50 nM immediately before measurement in a gasket on the coverslip and measure within seconds to minutes. Calibrate with standards of known mass (e.g. BSA, thyroglobulin, IgG). For tracking, conjugate small gold nanoparticles via monovalent linkers.
tips: Record a buffer-only measurement to measure background landing events.
Calibrate contrast-to-mass daily with known standards in the same buffer.
Adjust concentration so landing events are well separated in space and time.
Use ratiometric frame averaging appropriate to the landing rate.
For tracking, use the smallest gold label giving sufficient contrast to limit perturbation.
pitfalls: Buffer components (detergent micelles, glycerol inhomogeneities, lipids) give spurious mass peaks.
Membrane proteins, glycoproteins and nucleic acids have different refractive increments, shifting apparent mass.
Speckle from coverslip roughness masks small contrasts if background removal is inadequate.
Particles moving axially show changing and inverted contrast.
Surface binding preference or dissociation at low concentration distorts oligomer distributions.

quiz.q: Why does iSCAT contrast scale with d³ rather than d⁶?
quiz.a: The detected signal is dominated by the cross term between reference and scattered fields, which is linear in the scattered field amplitude, and that amplitude scales with polarizability, i.e. volume. Dark-field detects |E_s|², which scales as d⁶.

quiz.q: What fundamentally limits detection of small proteins?
quiz.a: Shot noise of the reference light: detecting contrast c needs ~1/c² photons per spot, plus residual background from coverslip roughness and instabilities. High photon flux, large-well cameras, frame averaging and reference attenuation help.

quiz.q: How would you use mass photometry in a protein biochemistry project?
quiz.a: Measure oligomeric distributions and complex formation in solution at nM concentrations with small volumes, after calibrating with known standards, and compare with SEC-MALS or native MS. Be aware of refractive increment differences for glycosylated or lipid-associated proteins.

tagline: Low-coherence interferometry measures the echo time delay of backscattered light, giving micrometre-scale depth sections of tissue down to 1-2 mm, the optical equivalent of ultrasound.
principle: Light travels too fast to time echoes directly, so OCT uses interferometry. A broadband (low temporal coherence) source is split between a reference arm and the sample. Light backscattered from structures in the sample interferes with reference light only when the optical path lengths match within the coherence length. The axial resolution is therefore set by the coherence length, which is inversely proportional to the source bandwidth, not by the objective NA.

In time-domain OCT the reference mirror is moved and the interference envelope traces the depth profile (A-scan). Fourier-domain OCT, now standard, keeps the reference fixed and records the interference spectrum; a Fourier transform of the spectral fringes gives the full depth profile at once because each depth produces a fringe frequency proportional to its path difference. Spectral-domain OCT uses a broadband source and a spectrometer with a line camera; swept-source OCT uses a rapidly tuned laser and a single detector. Fourier-domain detection gives a sensitivity advantage of roughly 20-30 dB, enabling A-scan rates of tens of kHz to MHz.

Lateral resolution is set separately by the focusing optics, as in any microscope. Because OCT typically uses low-NA beams for long depth of field, lateral resolution is ~5-20 µm; optical coherence microscopy (OCM) and full-field OCT use high NA for cellular resolution at the cost of depth of field.

Imaging depth is limited by scattering to ~1-2 mm in most tissues, extended by longer wavelengths (1300 nm, 1700 nm). Functional extensions include Doppler OCT for blood flow, OCT angiography (decorrelation of repeated B-scans maps perfused vessels without dyes), polarization-sensitive OCT for birefringence of collagen and nerve fibres, and visible-light OCT for oximetry.

OCT is a clinical standard in ophthalmology (retinal layer thickness, macular degeneration, glaucoma) and is used in cardiology (intravascular OCT), dermatology, and in biology for imaging embryos, zebrafish, organoids and brain tissue.
light_path: A broadband source (superluminescent diode, supercontinuum or femtosecond laser for SD-OCT; swept laser for SS-OCT), centred at e.g. 840, 1060 or 1300 nm.
A fibre coupler (Michelson or Mach-Zehnder) splits light into reference and sample arms.
In the sample arm, galvanometer scanners and a scan lens focus the beam into tissue and scan it laterally to form B-scans and volumes.
Backscattered sample light and reference light recombine in the coupler.
In SD-OCT a spectrometer disperses the light onto a line camera; in SS-OCT a balanced photodetector records interference versus time as the laser sweeps.
The spectrum is resampled to linear wavenumber, dispersion-compensated and Fourier transformed to give A-scans.

equations.name: Axial resolution (Gaussian spectrum)
equations.formula: Δz = (2 ln 2 / π) · λ0² / Δλ ≈ 0.44 λ0²/Δλ (in air; divide by n in tissue)
equations.meaning: Broader bandwidth Δλ gives finer depth resolution; e.g. 840 nm with 50 nm bandwidth gives ~6 µm in air.

equations.name: Lateral resolution
equations.meaning: Gaussian beam focused by lens of focal length f with beam diameter D.

equations.name: Depth of field
equations.meaning: Twice the Rayleigh range; finer lateral resolution means shorter depth of field.

equations.name: Maximum imaging range (SD-OCT)
equations.meaning: Set by spectral sampling interval δλ per camera pixel.

equations.name: Spectral interferogram
equations.formula: I(k) ∝ S(k) [R_r + Σ R_s,i + 2 Σ √(R_r R_s,i) cos(2k Δz_i)]
equations.meaning: Each reflector at depth Δz_i creates fringes with frequency proportional to Δz_i; Fourier transform recovers depth.

strengths: Label-free, non-contact depth imaging with µm axial resolution.
Very fast volumetric imaging in vivo.
Functional extensions: flow, angiography, birefringence.
Mature clinical technology.
limitations: No molecular contrast; signal is backscattering.
Penetration limited to ~1-2 mm.
Speckle noise reduces image quality.
Trade-off between lateral resolution and depth of field.
best_for: Retinal and anterior eye imaging.
Skin, oral and intravascular imaging.
Embryo, zebrafish and organoid morphology and heart dynamics.
Label-free angiography and blood flow.
sample_prep: No labelling needed. For ex vivo or small-animal work, keep tissue hydrated and minimise motion (anaesthesia, mounting in agarose). Index-matching gel reduces surface reflections. For embryos, use stable temperature control.
tips: Match dispersion between reference and sample arms (hardware or numerical) to keep axial resolution at its theoretical value.
Place the region of interest near zero path delay but on one side to minimise sensitivity roll-off while avoiding mirror artefacts.
Average multiple B-scans or use angular/frequency compounding to reduce speckle.
Use motion correction and repeated scanning for angiography.
Calibrate axial scale with refractive index of the tissue.
pitfalls: Mirror (complex-conjugate) artefact folds structures across zero delay in Fourier-domain OCT.
Sensitivity roll-off with depth makes deep structures appear dimmer.
Dispersion mismatch broadens the axial PSF and blurs layers.
Shadowing below strongly scattering or absorbing structures (vessels) mimics missing tissue.
Motion artefacts and decorrelation noise in OCT angiography.

quiz.q: Why does OCT axial resolution not depend on NA?
quiz.a: Depth is resolved by coherence gating: interference occurs only when path lengths match within the coherence length, which depends on source bandwidth (Δz ≈ 0.44λ0²/Δλ). The objective sets only lateral resolution.

quiz.q: Why is Fourier-domain OCT more sensitive than time-domain OCT?
quiz.a: All depths are measured simultaneously: each spectral channel integrates signal from all depths while shot noise is spread across spectral channels, giving a sensitivity gain proportional to the number of spectral pixels, typically 20-30 dB.

quiz.q: What is the mirror artefact in FD-OCT?
quiz.a: The Fourier transform of a real spectrum is symmetric, so structures at +Δz and −Δz cannot be distinguished; sample must be placed on one side of zero delay or complex-conjugate removal techniques used.

tagline: Short laser pulses absorbed in tissue cause thermoelastic expansion that launches ultrasound waves, so optical absorption contrast can be imaged at depths far beyond the optical diffusion limit.
principle: When a short light pulse is absorbed, the local temperature rises slightly and the tissue expands, producing an initial pressure rise p0 = Γ μ_a F, where μ_a is the absorption coefficient, F the local fluence and Γ the Grüneisen parameter (~0.1-0.25 in soft tissue). This pressure propagates as broadband ultrasound, which is detected by transducers at the surface. Because ultrasound scatters about 1000 times less than light in tissue, the absorbers can be localized acoustically even where light is fully diffuse.

Efficient signal generation requires the pulse to be shorter than both the thermal relaxation time (heat diffusion out of the voxel) and the stress relaxation time (sound leaving the voxel), so-called thermal and stress confinement; nanosecond pulses satisfy this for µm to mm structures.

Photoacoustic microscopy (PAM) uses focused optics or transducers. In optical-resolution PAM the laser is focused tightly, giving µm lateral resolution (set by optics) at depths up to ~1 mm; acoustic-resolution PAM uses a focused ultrasound transducer, giving tens of µm resolution at several mm. Photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) uses arrays of transducers and image reconstruction (e.g. back-projection or model-based inversion) to image centimetres deep with sub-mm resolution. Across the scale range the ratio of depth to resolution is roughly 100-200.

Contrast comes from optical absorption: oxy- and deoxyhaemoglobin (allowing oxygen saturation sO2 imaging by multiwavelength unmixing), melanin, lipids and water at near-IR bands, and exogenous agents such as ICG, gold nanorods, and genetically encoded reporters (near-IR fluorescent proteins and photoswitchable bacterial phytochromes). This makes it powerful for vascular, oxygenation and tumour imaging in small animals and patients.

Quantitation is complicated because the signal depends on the local fluence, which decays with depth in a wavelength-dependent way (spectral colouring), and on acoustic propagation through heterogeneous tissue.
light_path: A pulsed laser (Q-switched Nd:YAG with OPO, or ns diode/fibre lasers) produces ~5-10 ns pulses, tunable in the visible to near-IR.
Light is delivered to tissue through free-space optics or fibres: tightly focused (OR-PAM) or broadly illuminating (PACT).
Absorbed light generates ultrasound; acoustic coupling via water or gel transmits it to the transducer.
A single focused transducer (PAM, mechanically scanned) or an array (linear, ring or hemispherical for PACT) detects the waves.
Signals are amplified, digitised and reconstructed into images; multiwavelength data are spectrally unmixed.

resolution.z: ~10-100 µm (set by ultrasound bandwidth); scales with transducer frequency
resolution.why: Lateral resolution comes from optical focus (OR-PAM) or acoustic focus/aperture (AR-PAM, PACT); axial resolution from ultrasound bandwidth; depth limited by light attenuation and ultrasound frequency attenuation.

strengths: Optical absorption contrast at depths beyond optical microscopy.
Label-free imaging of haemoglobin concentration and oxygen saturation.
Scalable from cells (OR-PAM) to organs (PACT).
Compatible with ultrasound imaging for anatomical co-registration.
limitations: Only absorbers give contrast; scattering structures do not.
Quantitation affected by unknown fluence and spectral colouring.
Acoustic coupling needed; bone and air strongly disrupt sound.
Reconstruction artefacts from limited view and bandwidth.
best_for: Vascular imaging, angiogenesis and oxygen saturation in tumours and brain.
Small-animal whole-body functional imaging.
Melanoma and lymph node imaging.
Imaging genetically encoded near-IR reporters in deep tissue.
sample_prep: No labels required for haemoglobin or melanin contrast. Remove hair, couple transducers with ultrasound gel or water, and keep animals anaesthetised and warm. For exogenous contrast, inject agents such as ICG or nanoparticles; for genetically encoded contrast, express near-IR proteins (iRFP, BphP1).
tips: Use multiple wavelengths and fluence correction models when estimating sO2.
Ensure adequate acoustic coupling (no bubbles) and correct speed of sound in reconstruction.
Average pulses to improve SNR and correct for pulse-to-pulse energy fluctuations with a reference photodiode.
Use full-view geometries or model-based reconstruction to reduce limited-view artefacts.
Keep fluence within safety limits.
pitfalls: Spectral colouring: wavelength-dependent attenuation of fluence with depth biases unmixed sO2 and concentrations.
Limited-view and limited-bandwidth artefacts: structures parallel to the array or large uniform objects appear as edges only.
Speed-of-sound mismatch blurs and distorts images.
Reflections and reverberations create ghost structures.
Motion between wavelengths corrupts spectral unmixing.

quiz.q: Why can photoacoustic imaging see deeper than optical microscopy?
quiz.a: Contrast comes from optical absorption, but localization uses ultrasound, which scatters about three orders of magnitude less than light in tissue. Even when light is diffuse, the acoustic waves carry spatial information.

quiz.q: What are the stress and thermal confinement conditions?
quiz.a: The laser pulse must be shorter than the time for sound to leave the voxel (stress) and for heat to diffuse away (thermal), so energy builds up as pressure; ns pulses fulfil both for µm-mm features.

quiz.q: Why is sO2 quantitation at depth difficult?
quiz.a: The signal is Γμ_aF, and fluence F decreases with depth differently at each wavelength because of haemoglobin absorption and scattering (spectral colouring), so simple unmixing of raw spectra is biased; fluence modelling or calibration is needed.
